name: Rolling Forecasts
title: Rolling Forecasts
answer: A rolling forecast is a financial projection that is continually extended as time passes, so that the planning horizon stays a fixed distance ahead rather than shrinking toward a year end. Instead of a single annual budget that ages, the model is refreshed each period, typically monthly or quarterly, and the oldest period drops off as a new one is added. In practice it sits alongside the statutory budget and the long range plan, and it is used for steering rather than for the formal accounts. The scope covers revenue, cost, cash and headcount lines at whatever granularity the business can actually maintain.

sections.body: A rolling forecast is a financial projection that is continually extended as time passes, so that the planning horizon stays a fixed distance ahead rather than shrinking toward a year end. Instead of a single annual budget that ages, the model is refreshed each period, typically monthly or quarterly, and the oldest period drops off as a new one is added. The scope covers revenue, cost, cash and headcount lines at whatever granularity the business can actually maintain.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the same planning platforms that hold the budget, whether that is a dedicated tool such as Anaplan, Oracle EPM or Workday Adaptive Planning, or a spreadsheet model kept under version control. It needs a clean feed from the general ledger and from the operational systems that drive the drivers, such as order books, pipeline, headcount and utilisation. A defined calendar matters as much as the software, because the refresh has to land before the management pack is circulated. Most teams also keep a documented driver map so that a change in one assumption flows through consistently.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The forecast is built from drivers rather than from last year plus a percentage, so volume, price, mix and headcount each carry their own assumption. The common pattern is a short actuals period, a detailed forecast for the next few months and a lighter one beyond, with the far periods held at a coarser level. Variance analysis against the prior forecast and against budget is what gives the numbers meaning, and the assumptions behind each movement are recorded so they can be revisited. Where machine learning is used, it usually sits on the revenue or demand line, with the cost and cash build still driven by rules and judgement.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Because a rolling forecast is refreshed often, the controls around it have to be lighter than those around the statutory budget but still real. Version control, an audit trail of who changed which assumption, and a clear owner for each line are the basics. The provenance of the data matters, so the link back to the ledger and to source systems should be traceable, and any manual override should be visible rather than buried. Where the forecast feeds external guidance or covenant reporting, it falls under the same review and sign off as any other published figure.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward shorter cycles and more automation, with the refresh moving from monthly toward weekly or continuous in businesses that have the data to support it. Driver based models are being paired with statistical and machine learning components, which shifts the accountant's role toward validating assumptions and explaining variance rather than building every line by hand. Scenario and sensitivity views are becoming a standard part of the pack, so that a single point forecast is no longer the only output. The constraint is rarely the software, it is the quality of the underlying data and the willingness of the business to commit to a set of drivers.
